newsitem.title: UK: UK gives details of proposed Welsh assembly.
newsitem.headline: UK gives details of proposed Welsh assembly.

text.p: The British government unveiled plans on Tuesday for a 60-strong Welsh assembly with a seven billion pound ($11.7 billion) budget and power over schools, hospitals and other services in a nation of three million people.

The assembly, which will be elected in May 1999 if there is a positive response in a referendum to be held on September 18, puts flesh on the bones of Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair's commitment to devolve power from London to the regions.
Details of plans for a Scottish parliament, which unlike the Welsh assembly will have the power to raise or cut taxes, will be published on Thursday.

"This government is pledged to clean up and modernise British politics. We believe it is right to decentralise power, to open up government, to reform parliament and to increase individual rights," Blair said in the foreword to a paper setting out his government's plans for Wales.
Wales will remain firmly a part of the United Kingdom, sharing a common legal system with England, and will continue to return 40 members to the London parliament.
The new assembly will be located in the capital, Cardiff and will take over most of the powers and funding now in the hands of the Welsh Office.
Most of the Welsh Office's 2,000 civil servants will transfer to the assembly, which Blair wants to spearhead a development plan to bring more jobs to Wales.

Critics say the assembly will be just a talking shop -- in English and Welsh, the country's ancient Celtic tongue -- and the government acknowledges that the Welsh Secretary, Ron Davies, will not be bound by its views.
But Davies, who will continue to sit in Blair's cabinet, said it offered Wales a new beginning alongside other successful regions in Europe to set out its own strategic priorities.
"An elected assembly will give Wales a voice -- in Britain and Europe -- after years of neglect," he wrote in the paper. "It is an opportunity we must have the confidence to grasp."
Forty members of the assembly will be elected by the first-past-the-post voting system used in national elections.
The other twenty will be chosen by proportional representation through the additional member system used in Germany and elsewhere.
Among its powers, the assembly will be able to reduce the number of 80 unelected bodies that deliver services worth two billion pounds a year and hold them to account.
It will also exercise Davies's current responsibilties for health, education, industry and training, agriculture, environment, roads, planning, arts and culture.
The assembly will not have any say in areas outside the Welsh secretary's remit. The Home Office (interior ministry), for example, will continue to set prisons policy for the whole of Britain.
Opinion polls suggest a majority in favour of a Welsh assembly, in contrast to 1979, when similar proposals by the last Labour government were rejected by a four-to-one margin.
But some Labour members of parliament plan to risk the wrath of their leaders by campaigning for a No vote on September 18.

"As a socialist, I am saying no to a Welsh assembly because in my opinion it is going to take us down the road of nationalism, separatism and all the ugliness that goes with that," devolution dissident Llew Smith told BBC Radio Wales.
